lesson.title: The Power of Believing: The Placebo Effect
lesson.summary: The placebo effect is the genuine improvement a subject experiences from believing they received real treatment, even when they actually received an inactive placebo, and it is why credible experiments require a placebo controlled comparison.
lesson.body:
The placebo effect is the measurable improvement in a subject's condition that results from the subject's belief that they are receiving a real, effective treatment, even when the treatment they actually received was an inactive placebo. It is a genuine psychological and sometimes physiological response, not a sign that the subject was imagining things or lying about their symptoms.

The placebo effect is exactly what the allergy medication example from the previous section demonstrated: 41 out of 100 subjects who received nothing but an inert pill still reported feeling better, a 41% improvement rate driven entirely by expectation, ritual, and belief. Without a placebo group built into the experiment, that 41% would have been invisible, and researchers might have wrongly credited the full 68% improvement rate in the medication group to the drug's chemistry, when in fact a substantial share of it, roughly 41 percentage points worth, was likely present regardless of whether subjects received the real drug.

The size of the placebo effect varies a great deal depending on what is being measured. Pain and mood related outcomes tend to show large placebo responses because they are influenced heavily by a subject's expectations and nervous system, while an outcome like a specific measurable lab value in blood work tends to show a much smaller placebo response because it does not depend much on what the subject believes. Suppose two separate placebo controlled trials each enroll 100 subjects. In a headache pain trial, the placebo group might report a 35% reduction in pain, while in a trial measuring a cholesterol lab value, the placebo group might show only a 2% change. Both are placebo effects, but their size tells researchers something about how psychologically sensitive the particular outcome being measured actually is.

Because the placebo effect can be large, any well-designed experiment testing a treatment on subjects must include a placebo controlled control group, otherwise the treatment's apparent effect is confounded with the placebo effect, and the two cannot be separated. This is a direct extension of the reasoning behind treatments and control groups: the placebo effect is precisely the kind of hidden force that a placebo controlled comparison exists to neutralize. Researchers have also found that the form a placebo takes changes how strong the effect is: a placebo injection tends to produce a larger placebo response than a placebo pill, and a larger, more impressive looking pill tends to produce a larger placebo response than a small plain one, both patterns consistent with the idea that expectation, not chemistry, is what is driving the improvement.

The placebo effect is also why blinding, keeping subjects unaware of which treatment they received, matters so much. A subject who knows they received the real drug may report feeling better partly because they expect to, while a subject who knows they received a placebo may not experience much of a placebo effect at all precisely because they know it is fake, which is why the strongest experiments keep this information hidden from subjects for as long as the study runs.
